reasons: [coverage/major] D1 [criteriaAssessments C3; verdict; practicalImplications item 5; calculations (no LTV or 24-month calc)] The decision objective and C3 ask about net revenue and LTV, and G4 asks for a 24-month view. The draft only works out year-one break-even (K4, K10-K12) and says any LTV gain 'has to come in year two and later' without putting a number on it. The missing calculation is simple and decides the case. Monthly LTV at 3.2% churn is 49/0.032 = about $1,531, and annual LTV is 490/(1-r) for annual renewal rate r. The plan is LTV-neutral at r of about 68% for an average-churn converter. For a 1%-churn tenured converter, monthly LTV is about $4,900, so r must be at least about 90%. Without this renewal-rate threshold the test's success criterion is incomplete. The draft's vague 'renewal gains must recover about $94.75 per seat per year' cannot be acted on.

[coverage/major] D2 [criteriaAssessments C3; claims CL11; calculations K16] G4 asks for sensitivity at 10%, 20% and 30% conversion across converter mixes. The draft gives one extreme case: 30% conversion, all would-have-stayed (K16 = $29.40 per seat). It has no scenario grid with mixed shares of would-have-churned converters, so the decision-maker cannot see how the result moves with the two key unknowns. A grid can be computed with no new data, using the per-seat deltas the draft already has (-$98 for a stayer, roughly +$5 for a blended converter, gains for early churners).

[reasoning_validity/major] D3 [criteriaAssessments C2 (mechanisms), verdict, edgeCasesAndFailureModes[1], tradeoffs[3], correctedUserAssumptions[1]] The draft states as fact that the pilot's 91% is in-term retention inflated by prepaid lock-in, and that renewal 'was never measured' (C2 mechanisms, edgeCasesAndFailureModes item 2, tradeoffs item 4, verdict). Packet E4 explicitly flags the definition as unclear. A prepaid 12-month term should show near-zero in-term logo churn, so 9% churn within the term is odd. The 2025 cohort's '12-month retention' may well be the month-12 renewal rate. If it is, 91% exceeds the roughly 68% LTV break-even renewal rate (see D1) and is materially favorable evidence, even allowing for selection. The draft resolves an open ambiguity in the direction that supports its conclusion, without justification.

[reasoning_validity/major] D4 [counterarguments[0].response; CL8] The first counterargument response says the company's 67.7% versus the pilot's 91% 'reproduces the same generic gap ... which is what selection alone would produce'. That does not follow. An observational gap that matches an industry observational gap says nothing about how it splits between selection and treatment, because the industry gap may itself contain a causal part (E12). Packet E10 says only that this 'suggests' the pilot is not proof of causation. The draft turns 'not proof of an effect' into 'consistent with no effect', which strawmans the strongest pro-launch argument.

[reasoning_validity/major] D1 [furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion[0], [1]; compare verdict and C2] furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion items 1-2 say that confirming the pilot's 91% is a renewal rate, together with tenured monthly churn above about 0.9% (or tenured monthly retention of about 70-75%), 'would make the pilot favorable evidence and support a broader launch' and 'would imply a real causal effect'. That treats tenure-matching as enough to remove selection. Per E4, sales hand-picked the pilot accounts, which adds a second selection layer on top of tenure, and the draft itself says in C2 and CL6 that selection beyond observables cannot be ruled out (E11, the E12 limitations). This also contradicts the verdict, which allows scaling only after a randomized or holdout-controlled test. A decision-maker could skip the test after a quick internal data pull.

[decision_usefulness/major] D2 [verdict (Recommendation); practicalImplications[4], [5]; alternatives[0]] The recommendation ties scale-up to a measured month-12 renewal rate beating 1 - 10c. That metric cannot be observed for at least 12 months after enrollment, and enrollment itself runs up to 6 months per E2. The draft gives no test size, though at n=40 the Wilson interval is 78-97% (K43, K44), which cannot separate the 68%/90%/92% thresholds the draft sets. It also gives no interim leading indicators (uptake rate, converter tenure mix versus the 66% would-have-stayed threshold in K33, in-term seat contraction) and no interim decision rule. The decision-maker does not learn what to do in the next 12-18 months or how many accounts the test needs.

[reasoning_validity/critical] D1 [verdict step (4); practicalImplications[6] ('Final success rule'); alternatives[0]; tradeoffs[3]] The scale-up rule says to scale if month-12 renewal beats 1 - 10 x the holdout's measured monthly churn. That rule brings back the selection bias the draft warns about everywhere else. The break-even derived in K20/K22 uses c, the converter's own counterfactual monthly churn. A randomized holdout's average churn is the blended base rate (about 3.2%), so the threshold comes out near 68%. The draft itself argues that converters are likely tenured, lower-churn accounts, whose break-even is about 90-92% (K22, K23). Under the stated rule, a renewal rate of about 70-89% would pass even though it destroys LTV for a 1%-churn converter pool. The practical-implications bullet lists 68/90/92% as alternatives, but the operative rule in the verdict and in practicalImplications[6] fixes c as holdout churn. A correct rule would either (a) compare revenue per offered account against revenue per holdout account (intention-to-treat, the proper use of randomization), or (b) estimate c from holdout accounts matched to the converters' characteristics, such as tenure and seat count.

[reasoning_validity/major] D2 [K52; claim CL20; practicalImplications[4]; alternatives[0]; edgeCasesAndFailureModes[last]] K52 sizes the test to detect a 5-point difference in 12-month logo retention between offered and holdout arms (68% vs 73%). There are two problems. First, 12-month logo retention in the offered arm is pushed up mechanically by prepaid in-term lock-in, which the draft says elsewhere must not be the success metric (E17, practicalImplications[6]). Second, at 10-30% uptake, a 5-point difference between arms means converters would need a retention gain of about 17-50 points, so the sizing does not match a plausible effect size. Sizing the test on per-account revenue or retention measured after renewal (for example at 24 months) would match the draft's own decision logic. The stated feasibility figure of about 1,302 accounts per arm, and the conclusion drawn from it, are therefore unreliable.

[decision_usefulness/major] D3 [verdict step (3); practicalImplications[5]; furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion[2]] The month-6 interim rule says to pause if more than about 64-66% of converters 'would have stayed'. That counterfactual cannot be observed. The draft substitutes an undefined proxy, 'tenured accounts with no churn-risk signals', without saying how that proxy maps to would-have-stayed probability. The 64-66% threshold is also a year-one break-even only (K33, K48). Across a lifetime the plan can still lose value at a lower stayed share when renewal falls short of 1 - 10c, and gain value at a higher one when it exceeds it. As written, the interim gate cannot be put into practice and may conflict with the lifetime rule.
